These topics are adjacent to the profile's experience in autonomy, trajectory planning, simulation, navigation, and mission optimization, but the post does not specifically concern flight control or UAV systems.
signals.source_text: Navigation & Pathfinding has been completely reworked in UNIGINE Engine 2.22. The new experimental system is designed for large, dynamic worlds, with double-precision world coordinates to keep navigation accurate even across very large environments. Together, these improvements provide a much more scalable and flexible foundation for NPCs and other autonomous characters navigating complex simulation and game environments. You can now: • Generate NavMeshes automatically from scene geometry • Stream navigation data across large open worlds • Rebuild only affected areas when the environment changes • Generate navigation data at runtime for procedural or dynamic environments • Define cost-weighted areas, so characters can prefer roads, avoid rough terrain or hazards, and stay out of restricted zones • Handle dynamic obstacles without rebuilding the whole NavMesh • Use multithreaded pathfinding for large numbers of characters • Keep characters on route toward moving targets with path corridors • Run crowd avoidance with priorities and interaction rules • Profile navigation memory usage and per-frame performance directly in the engine For large-scale environments, you can also combine different levels of navigation detail — for example, keeping a coarse NavMesh for the whole world while streaming or generating higher-detail navigation around active characters. The new system is available as an experimental feature in UNIGINE SDK 2.22.
projects: Experimental Navigation & Pathfinding system in UNIGINE SDK 2.22
signals.content_angle: Develop an original technical comparison between large-world navigation architectures and autonomous vehicle mission planning, focusing on dynamic obstacle updates, cost-weighted route selection, multiresolution maps, and performance profiling.

signals.source_text: In my last post here, I created a simulation of a robot arm (from Onshape by PTC ) that uses 4DOF and a pencil-like end effector to transcribe spoken or recorded audio into real Braille inside MathWorks Simscape. Braille characters are tactile reading symbols built from a standard six-dot cell arranged in two vertical columns of three dots. Naturally, I let my imagination run wild and created a tactile Braille reader too. It uses the same robot arm with an extra DOF that allows it to slide while reading, much like how real Braille would be read. It has three prongs on a finger that register a pulse anytime any prong touches a Braille dot. These pulses are converted into six-dot cells to form Unicode characters. Each character is sent with all previously read characters to the liblouis translator, which translates the Braille bytes back into readable English text. The most interesting lesson I learned while implementing this project is that the meaning of a Braille character can change depending on which characters are read before or after it! Cheers to learning new things every day. I just might end up trying this in hardware someday. Enjoy the demo below!

signals.source_text: What was the aircraft mass/MTOW, flight condition and power setting? Was this hover, take-off, approach or flyover? What was the measurement distance, microphone position and atmospheric condition? Was the test conducted in an acoustically open area, and how far away were the nearest reflecting surfaces? A single dB number is not an adequate description of aircraft noise. I would like to see the 1/3-octave-band SPL spectrum, together with the broadband and discrete tonal components. Propeller/rotor blade-passage frequencies and their harmonics can have a disproportionately high effect on perceived annoyance even when the overall SPL appears relatively modest. And the urban environment matters enormously. Buildings, façades and the ground introduce reflections, reverberation and, at particular frequencies and locations, constructive interference, producing local sound levels quite different from those measured in an open-field test. So comparing “<50 dB Valo” with “55 dB dishwasher” is visually attractive, but acoustically it is potentially very misleading. Noise is not just “how many dB?” It is how much, at what frequencies, for how long, under what operating condition, and measured where.

signals.source_text: How my docotoral journey began Six months ago, my doctoral thesis was finally published. I needed some distance first. Time to realise that this chapter was really finished and to put it away for a while. Now I’m ready to share its contents and findings. I also want to share some of the journey behind it, because pursuing a doctorate alongside my professional role was not always easy. Working between Munich and Tokyo for many years has given me first hand experience of how communication and relationship building differ across cultures. This experience shaped my research. Germany and Japan are both highly advanced manufacturing economies. What I wanted to understand was how decision makers build and sustain trust across a growing variety of communication channels. 💡 Which communication channels do decision makers and next generation professionals in German and Japanese SMEs actually use when buying machine tools or automation solutions, and why? 💡 What makes them trust one channel over another, and how do cultural and generational differences influence this? 💡 How do we maintain human connection as industrial communication becomes increasingly digital? For my research, I spoke with decision makers in Germany and Japan and also with the next generation who will make these decisions in the future. The findings confirmed something I had experienced throughout my professional life: industrial communication remains fundamentally shaped by human interaction, even as digitisation advances. I want to share this knowledge because these questions are relevant for our industry and I believe many companies are asking similar questions today. So this is the start of a series. Over the coming weeks, I will share some of the findings of my research and some reflections of my journey.
